source: daywave 2026-10-27 film art music wave 2, from the local wave2-film cache

rows.title: The World Is Not Enough
rows.evidence: The filming section says that after the title sequence, Eilean Donan Castle in Scotland is used by MI6 as a location headquarters, and that filming at Eilean Donan Castle depicted the exterior of the temporary operations centre Castle Thane. The Eilean Donan article says that in 1999 the castle served as the Scottish headquarters of MI6 in this film.
rows.summary: The World Is Not Enough uses Eilean Donan Castle as an MI6 location headquarters. The filming section says the castle depicts the exterior of the temporary operations centre called Castle Thane. The Eilean Donan article says that in 1999 the castle served as the Scottish headquarters of MI6 in the film.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, the exterior the articles name as the filming location.

rows.title: Black Angel
rows.evidence: The Eilean Donan article says the castle was the setting for the 1980 short film Black Angel, filmed to accompany screenings of The Empire Strikes Back.
rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the castle was the setting for the 1980 short film Black Angel, made to accompany cinema screenings of The Empire Strikes Back.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, which the article names as the setting.

rows.title: Bonnie Prince Charlie
rows.evidence: The Eilean Donan article says the castle has appeared in films, beginning with Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1948.
rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the castle has made several film appearances, beginning with Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1948.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, the location the article names in that film appearance.

rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says film appearances of the castle begin with Bonnie Prince Charlie in 1948 and The Master of Ballantrae in 1953.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, the location the article names in that film appearance.

rows.evidence: The Eilean Donan article says the castle featured in the opening episode of the 1976 television series The New Avengers.
rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the castle featured in the opening episode of the 1976 television series The New Avengers.

rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the castle featured prominently in Mio in the Land of Faraway (1987), where it stands in as a home in the story.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, which the article says featured in the film.

rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says that in 2007 the castle stood in for Fotheringhay Castle in Elizabeth: The Golden Age.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, the place the article says stood in for Fotheringhay.

rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the castle appears in Made of Honor as the home of the groom's family.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, which the article says appears in the film.

rows.evidence: The Eilean Donan article says that in 1984 Jesse Rae filmed his music video Over The Sea at the castle.
rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says that in 1984 the music video Over The Sea was filmed at the castle.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, where the article says the video was filmed.

rows.title: Kandukondain Kandukondain
rows.evidence: The Eilean Donan article says the Tamil song Kandukondain Kandukondain, from the film of the same name, was filmed at the castle.
rows.summary: The Eilean Donan article says the Tamil song Kandukondain Kandukondain, from the film of the same name, was filmed at the castle.
rows.image_note: Photograph of Eilean Donan Castle, where the article says the song was filmed.

rows.title: Alasdair Crotach's wall tomb
rows.evidence: The article says St Clement's Church is in Rodel, Harris, and that in 1528 Alasdair Crotach MacLeod prepared a wall tomb on the south side of the choir, crowned by an arch and carved with biblical scenes.
rows.summary: St Clement's Church is in Rodel, on Harris. The article says that in 1528 Alasdair Crotach MacLeod prepared a wall tomb on the south side of the choir, crowned by an arch and carved with biblical scenes, and calls it possibly the finest medieval wall tomb in Scotland.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the carved wall tomb, with the arched biblical panels and the effigy.

rows.title: St Cormac's Chapel
rows.evidence: The article says Eilean Mòr in the MacCormaig Isles has a chapel built in the 13th century and altered in the 14th century, a rectangular building about 11.5 by 6 metres.
rows.summary: Eilean Mòr, in the MacCormaig Isles near Loch Sween, has St Cormac's Chapel. The article says the chapel is a rectangular building about 11.5 by 6 metres, built in the 13th century and altered in the 14th century, when the chancel was upgraded.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the chapel. A standing stone is in the foreground; the carving the article describes on St Cormac's Cross is not visible on it.

rows.title: Papil Stone
rows.evidence: The article says the Papil Stone is an 8th-century Pictish cross-slab from a religious site at Papil, West Burra, Shetland, and that it is now in the National Museum of Scotland. It describes the cross, the quadruped, and the bird-headed figures with axes at the base.
rows.summary: The Papil Stone is an 8th-century carved Pictish cross-slab from a religious site at Papil on West Burra, Shetland. The article describes a cross, clerics, a quadruped, and two bird-headed figures with axes flanking a human head. It is now displayed in the National Museum of Scotland.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the Papil Stone, showing the cross, the quadruped, and the axe-bearing figures the article describes.

rows.title: Oronsay High Cross
rows.evidence: The article says Oronsay Priory stood on the island of Oronsay in the Inner Hebrides, and that the High Cross east of the church has a crucifixion on its westward side and recalls Prior Colin, probably in 1510.
rows.summary: Oronsay Priory was a house of canons on the island of Oronsay, in the Inner Hebrides. The article says the High Cross stands about four metres east of the church, recalls the death of Prior Colin in about 1510, and has a crucifixion on its westward side.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the crucifixion on the westward side of the High Cross.

rows.title: Nendrum sundial
rows.evidence: The article says Nendrum Monastery was on Mahee Island in Strangford Lough, and that the canonical sundial at a corner of the ruined church was reconstructed from fragments found in 1924 and dated to about the year 900.
rows.summary: Nendrum Monastery stood on Mahee Island in Strangford Lough. The article says the canonical sundial at one corner of the ruined church was reconstructed from fragments found in the 1924 excavation and has been dated to about the year 900.
rows.commons_file: File:Sun Dial Nendrum Monastery Ruins - geograph.org.uk - 346240.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of the sundial at the corner of the ruined church.

rows.title: Tau Cross
rows.evidence: The Tory Island article says the Tau Cross, a T-shaped cross, is believed to date from the 12th century and is one of only two tau crosses in Ireland.
rows.summary: On Tory Island, the article describes the Tau Cross, a T-shaped cross believed to date from the 12th century. It says this is one of only two tau crosses in Ireland, the other being at Kilnaboy in County Clare.
rows.commons_file: File:Tau Cross and West Pier, Toraigh - geograph.org.uk - 1437370.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of the Tau Cross beside the west pier.

rows.title: Baptism Church
rows.evidence: The Inis Cealtra article says the small Romanesque Baptism Church is enclosed by a stone wall and that its doorway is an arch of three orders.
rows.reject_reason: The Inis Cealtra article describes the small Romanesque Baptism Church, enclosed by a stone wall, with a doorway of three orders. It never uses the name St Brigid's. The photograph's file title and Commons description call the foreground ruin St Brigid's Church, with St Caimin's Church behind it. The article does not say those are the same building, so the picture is not shown to be the Baptism Church.
rows.summary: Inis Cealtra, also called Holy Island, is in Lough Derg. The article says the small Romanesque Baptism Church is enclosed by a stone wall and that its doorway is an arch of three orders. It says the church was blown down in 1839.
rows.commons_file: File:Holy Island Clare St. Brigids Church.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of the Romanesque doorway. The file title calls this church St Brigid's; the article calls the Romanesque church the Baptism Church. The roofed church and round tower behind it are St. Caimin's Church and the round tower.

rows.title: Round tower
rows.evidence: The Inis Cealtra article says the island has an Irish round tower, that its cone-cap was not found, and that restoration was carried out between 1970 and 1980.
rows.summary: Inis Cealtra has an Irish round tower. The article says the cone-cap was not found, which fits the legend that the tower was never finished, and that restoration was carried out between 1970 and 1980. It calls St. Caimin's Church the only roofed building.
rows.commons_file: File:Holy Island Clare St. Caimin's and Brigid's churches.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of the round tower, with the flat top the article's missing cone-cap describes. The roofed building beside it is St. Caimin's Church. The ruined Romanesque church is also in the frame.

rows.title: Carved slabs
rows.evidence: The Caher Island article says the island, between Clare Island and Inishturk, has an early Christian monastery with a chapel in an enclosure and several carved slabs.
rows.summary: Caher Island, off County Mayo between Clare Island and Inishturk, has an early Christian monastery. The article says the remains include a chapel in an enclosure and several carved slabs.
rows.commons_file: File:One of the crosses on Caher Island, Co Mayo, Ireland.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of one standing carved stone on Caher Island. The carving of a figure is weathered. The file title calls it one of the crosses; the article calls these carved slabs.

rows.title: Bressay Stone
rows.evidence: The Bressay article calls the Bressay Stone an outstanding piece of Pictish art: a chlorite-slate slab about 16 inches wide at the top, with ogham on the sides, a cross on each face, two men with crosiers, horses, pigs, and a figure between sea monsters.
rows.reject_reason: The article describes that small ogham slab. The cached photograph titled as the Bressay Stone in St Mary's walls is a blurred churchyard slab and does not show the ogham edges, the two clerics, or the sea monsters. Bressay Crosses St Mary's Church is a different churchyard cross. Bressay Stone Replica is a replica. The Archaeological Journal plate is an illustration, not a photograph of the stone.
rows.summary: The Bressay article describes the Bressay Stone as a Pictish slab of chlorite slate, about 16 inches wide at the top, with ogham on the slender sides, knotwork, a cross on each face, two men with crosiers, horses, pigs, and a figure shown between sea monsters.
rows.commons_file: File:Bressay Stone in St Mary's Walls - geograph.org.uk - 2059923.jpg
rows.image_note: Photograph of a slab by the ruined walls at St Mary's. It does not show the Bressay Stone the article describes.

rows.title: Baloo Baleerie
rows.evidence: The article says Baloo Baleerie is also known as the Bressay Lullaby because it is based on a BBC recording made on 22 January 1949 on Bressay.
rows.reject_reason: The article does place the 1949 recording on Bressay. The cached photographs are carved stones at St Mary's, a replica of the Bressay Stone, and a journal illustration. None is a photograph of the lullaby or of that recording.
rows.summary: Baloo Baleerie is a Scottish lullaby. The article says the title comes from the Scots word baloo, and that it is also called the Bressay Lullaby because a BBC recording was made on Bressay on 22 January 1949. Alan Lomax published it in 1951.

rows.title: St Cormac's Cross
rows.evidence: The article says St Cormac's Cross stands beside the chapel and is believed to date from the 10th century. The east face has beak-headed monsters, a hooded rider, and a monster gripping a snake.
rows.reject_reason: The article describes those carvings on St Cormac's Cross. The cached chapel photograph includes a standing stone, but the beak-headed monsters, hooded rider, and other carving are not visible. The cache has no photograph of the carved cross.
rows.summary: Beside St Cormac's Chapel on Eilean Mòr, the article describes St Cormac's Cross, believed to be 10th-century. Only the shaft and the lower part of the ring survive. The east face has wrestling beak-headed monsters, a hooded rider on an oversized horse, and a monster gripping a snake.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the chapel. The standing stone in the foreground does not show the carving the article describes.

rows.title: St Cormac's Cave
rows.evidence: The article says St Cormac's Cave, on the south end of Eilean Mòr, has two incised crosses on its east wall, dated by their style to about 700.
rows.reject_reason: The article places the incised crosses inside the cave. The cached photograph's own description says the cave lies just behind the rough wall and that the crosses are inside. The wall is in the frame, not the crosses.
rows.summary: St Cormac's Cave is on the south end of Eilean Mòr. The article says the cave is about 3 metres long and has two incised crosses on its east wall, dated by their style to about 700. A rough stone wall in front may have controlled access.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the wall in front of the cave. The file description says the crosses are inside, behind the wall.

rows.title: Southcairn carvings
rows.evidence: The Holm of Papa article says the Southcairn is a chambered cairn of about 3000 BC whose stones carry ancient carvings, including eyebrow-motif carvings in the southernmost chamber.
rows.reject_reason: The article describes the carvings inside the Southcairn. The cached photograph is a distant view of the holm from the water. The cairn carvings are not in the frame.
rows.summary: The Holm of Papa, also called the Holm of Papay, lies just east of Papa Westray. The article says the Southcairn is a stalled chambered cairn of about 3000 BC, and that eyebrow-motif carvings in its southern chamber resemble the eyes of the Orkney Venus.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the Holm of Papa from across the water, not of the cairn carvings. The file record has no machine-readable author; its Commons categories include Photos by Drew Corser.

rows.title: Macdara's Church
rows.evidence: The article says the present stone church replaced a wooden church, that the roof stones were cut to mimic wood shingles, and that the building is dated to the 10th century.
rows.reject_reason: The church is in the frame, but the photograph is a pilgrimage crowd and many people are identifiable. The project does not use that picture, and the cache has no other photograph of the church.
rows.summary: Saint Macdara's Island, off Carna in County Galway, has a stone church dated to the 10th century. The article says an earlier wooden church was replaced by this building, and that the roof stones were cut to mimic wooden shingles.
rows.image_note: Photograph of the church on the feast day, with a crowd of people in the frame.

rows.title: O'Malley Tomb
rows.evidence: The Clare Island article says Clare Island Abbey contains the O'Malley Tomb, a possible burial site of Gráinne O'Malley.
rows.reject_reason: The article places the O'Malley Tomb inside Clare Island Abbey. The cached photograph is a north-east exterior of the abbey. The tomb is not in the frame. The wall-tomb photograph in this cache is Alasdair Crotach's tomb at Rodel, on Harris.
rows.summary: Clare Island Abbey, near the south coast, was founded by the O'Malleys. The article says it contains the O'Malley Tomb, a possible burial site of Gráinne O'Malley.

open_image.attribution: Andreas F. Borchert, via Wikimedia Commons

rows.image_note: Photograph of the abbey exterior, not of the tomb.

rows.title: Medieval roof paintings
rows.evidence: The Clare Island article says the abbey is known for its rare medieval roof paintings.
rows.reject_reason: The article names the medieval roof paintings in the abbey. The cached photograph is a north-east exterior of the building. The paintings are not in the frame.
rows.summary: The Clare Island article says Clare Island Abbey is known for its rare medieval roof paintings.

open_image.attribution: Andreas F. Borchert, via Wikimedia Commons

rows.image_note: Photograph of the abbey exterior, not of the roof paintings.

rows.title: Budawanny
rows.evidence: The Clare Island article says the island is the setting for Bob Quinn's film Budawanny (1987).
rows.reject_reason: The article sets Budawanny on Clare Island. It does not name the abbey as a filming location. The only cached photograph is a north-east view of the abbey, a different landmark from the setting the sentence names.
rows.summary: The Clare Island article says the island is the setting for Bob Quinn's film Budawanny (1987). It also says he shot a documentary, The Island, there in 1966.

open_image.attribution: Andreas F. Borchert, via Wikimedia Commons

rows.image_note: Photograph of Clare Island Abbey, which the article does not tie to the film.

rows.title: Clare Island
rows.evidence: The Clare Island article says the island features in the song Clare Island by the Saw Doctors, from the 1996 album Same Oul' Town, where it is described as a haven from city life.
rows.reject_reason: The article does name the song and the island. The cached photograph is the abbey exterior, and the article does not connect the song to the abbey.
rows.summary: The Clare Island article says the island features in the Saw Doctors' song Clare Island, from the 1996 album Same Oul' Town, and that the song describes the island as a haven from city life.

open_image.attribution: Andreas F. Borchert, via Wikimedia Commons

rows.image_note: Photograph of Clare Island Abbey, not a photograph the article ties to the song.

rows.title: High crosses
rows.evidence: The Inis Cealtra article says the island has four high crosses, as well as the churches and the round tower.
rows.reject_reason: The article says there are four high crosses. The cached photographs show the Romanesque church, St. Caimin's Church, and the round tower. The high crosses are not the subject of those frames. A further church photograph is marked only as having no known copyright restrictions, which is not an open licence used here.
rows.summary: The Inis Cealtra article says the island has an Irish round tower, the ruins of several small churches, and four high crosses.

rows.title: Hostage Stone
rows.evidence: The Inchmarnock article describes the Hostage Stone, two conjoining pieces of incised slate from the early monastic site, with four human figures and a boat, read as a scene of hostage-taking or of a reliquary procession.
rows.reject_reason: The article names the Hostage Stone and places it on Inchmarnock. The cached Commons search for the stone returned no files, so there is no open-licence photograph of it.
rows.summary: The Inchmarnock article describes the Hostage Stone, found in the excavation north of St Marnock's church. Two joining fragments of incised slate show four human figures and a boat. One reading is a hostage-taking; another is a reliquary procession.

rows.title: Brooch of Lorn
rows.evidence: The article says the brooch was kept at Dunollie Castle and then moved to Gylen Castle on the island of Kerrera, and that it was taken when the castle was captured and burned in 1647.
rows.reject_reason: The article does say the brooch was kept at Gylen Castle on Kerrera until 1647. The cached Commons search returned no photograph of the brooch, and the brooch is not on the island now.
rows.summary: The Brooch of Lorn article says the brooch was kept at Dunollie and later moved to Gylen Castle on Kerrera during the Covenanter Wars. It says the castle was captured and burned in 1647 and the brooch was taken. The brooch is now with the MacDougall of Dunollie Preservation Trust.

rows.title: Stone crosses
rows.evidence: The Devenish Island article says there are examples of 15th-century stone crosses on the island, and describes the round tower of the monastery.
rows.reject_reason: The article names 15th-century stone crosses on Devenish. The wave-2 cache has no photograph of those crosses or of the round tower.
rows.summary: Devenish Island, in Lower Lough Erne, has an early Christian monastery and a round tower. The article says there are also examples of 15th-century stone crosses on the island.

rows.title: Cross slabs
rows.evidence: The Inishmurray article says the monastic site includes cross slabs among the churches, the stone-roofed oratory, and the enclosure.
rows.reject_reason: The article mentions cross slabs at the monastery. The wave-2 cache has no photograph of those slabs.
rows.summary: Inishmurray, off the County Sligo coast, has an early monastic enclosure. The article says the site includes churches, a stone-roofed oratory, and cross slabs.

rows.title: Poldark (2015 TV series)
rows.evidence: The production section lists filming locations in Cornwall, Bristol, Wiltshire, Somerset, Gloucestershire, and Bath. It does not name an atlas island. Dr Dwight Enys is a character, not an island in the article.
rows.reject_reason: The fetched article does not name an atlas island as a setting or a filming location.
rows.summary: The Poldark production notes list filming on the Cornish mainland and in Bristol, Wiltshire, Somerset, Gloucestershire, and Bath. They do not name an island in the atlas.
